Introduction
Study the past, if you would divine the future.
-- Confucius
Future shock is the shattering stress and disorientation that we induce
in individuals by subjecting them to too much change in too short a time.
-- Alvin Toffler
Norton Commander for DOS is the original line of Orthodox file managers that
exists in five major versions: 1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0 and 5.0. Only the last one has
an additional sub-version (nc 5.5). All versions are still used (mostly by DOS enthusiasts)
and are often posted on the abandonware sites. What is interesting, despite clear
superiority of later versions, there are still users of version 1.0 of NC. For example,
Symantec site contains an FAQ article:
Is Norton Commander Version 1.0 or 2.0 Supported Under Windows NT 5 (Beta)? .
Also in October of 2005 I received the following email addressed to me as an editor
of the OFM page at the Softpanorama website ( Orthodox
File Managers: Home of the OFM standards ):
Norton Commander 1.0
Hi,
I'm still using Norton Commander version 1.00 (1986) in Windows 98SE, even
in Windows 2000 Professional and Windows XP.
I prefer it's small size and fast, and I can write with it small batch programs.
Bye
Alvaro Alonso
From: Bogota, Colombia (South America)
It was probably one of the most popular file manager of the DOS era, which along
with Xtree remains one of the few
programs which managed to transcend their DOS roots and Norton Commander descendants
(OFM managers) now exist on all popular OSes. The first version of NC (1.0) was
designed and written by John Socha in 1984-1989. We provide a short biographical
notes about him later in this chapter .
Starting from version 2 Norton Commander got a cult following, somewhat comparable
with the success of 123, WordPerfect and MS Word, especially in former USSR and
Eastern Europe, where blue screen of Norton Commander became the synonym of DOS.
Many users from this region never suspected that this was not a native DOS interface.
In Russian the words "Norton" and "Commander" became part of PC jargon and are widely
used as synonyms for file manager. Please refer to Chapter
1 for more exploration of this phenomenon.
Norton Commander was taught as a part of introductory computer classes in most
of the former USSR region as well as Eastern European colleges and universities.
That means that all graduates were more or less knowledgeable Norton Commander users
and Norton Commander, in essence, served as standard interface for DOS. I would
like to stress it again that many people from this region never suspected that this
was not the part of DOS but an additional utility. In DOS days it even affected
hiring process: the mastery of Norton Commander was irrevocably linked with mastery
of DOS in minds of many Eastern European IT hiring managers.
The initial version of Norton Commander was called VDOS (Visual DOS)
and was written in a blend of C and assembler. As John Socha recollected
the events (personal communication):
I started work on what became known as the Norton Commander in the fall of
1984 while I was still a graduate student in Applied Physics at Cornell
University. The first versions were entirely in assembly language, but
that was too time-consuming, so I soon switched to a blend of C and assembly
language at a time when most "real programmers" wouldn't touch C.
At the time I called it Visual DOS, with the abbreviation of VDOS instead
of the usual two-letter abbreviations used at the time. The program
itself was inspired by several things coming together. I had a contract to write
some books for Microsoft Press and actually spent some time in Bellevue, WA
working on site. I'd take two months off from graduate school and write a book.
The second book was to be a book of small utility programs like I used to
write for Softalk Magazine (such as whereis, scrnsave, etc.), but I never
finished writing the book because one small utility took on a life of it's own.
John Socha received both MS and PhD in Applied Physics from Cornell University.
After graduation from the university John became the first director of research
and development for now defunct Peter Norton Computing. He was the second programmer
in the company, hired shortly after Brad Kingsbury.
At this time Peter Norton Computing was a one-man show. It was founded by
Peter Norton who was one
of the pioneer entrepreneurs in commercial PC software development. He formed his
company in 1982 with $30,000 and an IBM computer (the company was sold for 70 million
to Symantec in 1990; a nice return on investment). In 1992 Smart Computing paper
Investigating The Lost Files Of Peter Norton, PC Pioneer Gillian Coolidge wrote:
The story goes that Peter Norton worked in the aerospace industry back in
the late 1970s, but he lost his job when Boeing, McDonnell Douglas and Lockheed
all made severe cutbacks. To pay the bills, Norton took contract computer programming
jobs.
One day, Norton accidentally deleted an important file, a common-enough err

hn.title: What changes when your search index lives on S3?
hn.text:
Part 1 of a series on how Infino is built.
At Infino, we are building a retrieval engine to answer agent questions at scale, and its full-text search is among the fastest available [1] . Agents query structured, semi-structured and unstructured data, so we need to support SQL, vector search, BM25 full-text search, and any combination across these query shapes. In most cases, the data already resides in the object store, which guarantees scale and high availability. So, we decided to build the search index on the object store, supporting S3, GCS and Azure Blob Storage.
Search engines have traditionally kept their index on local disk. Lucene , which most search engines are built on or modeled after, assumes the index sits on a disk next to the CPU, where a random seek is relatively cheap. However, that is not the case when you move the index to object storage, where every random read is a network round-trip. In this post, we describe some of the design decisions we made differently because of that.
Architecture
Infino organizes the data into superfiles , which are Parquet files with Infino’s full-text and vector indexes. Many superfiles form a supertable . Each supertable has (a) a manifest , which lists superfiles along with their footers and index headers plus column statistics, and (b) a term index , which lists terms along with which superfiles they appear in and score bound information.
The cost model
On a local SSD, a random read costs nothing if a page is cached, and costs under a millisecond in case of a page fault. So a search engine whose index is on SSD can afford to make random reads liberally. On S3, GCS or Azure Blob, every random read is an HTTP GET request, which typically takes tens of milliseconds, and is billed in $$ per request, regardless of how many bytes it returns. This changes what you need to optimize when building a search engine on object storage. The scarcest resource is not CPU, and not bytes, but the number of round trips you make to the object store, and most design decisions below follow from that [2] .
One file per index unit
Search indexes are built as immutable units. You ingest a batch of documents, and the engine writes a self-contained index for them. Updates are written as new units too, and a background merge process later combines old units into new immutable units. In Lucene, the immutable unit is called a segment ; in Infino, it is called a superfile . The index data structures Infino uses are the topic of a later post, but a curious reader can read about them here: superfile architecture .
A Lucene segment is a set of files: a term dictionary ( .tim ), an index into the term dictionary ( .tip ), postings ( .doc ), positions ( .pos ), and so on. By default Lucene packs small segments into a compound file ( .cfs , with an entry table in .cfe ), while large segments keep their separate files. Either way, opening a segment on object storage takes several GET requests.
An Infino superfile is always a single object: a plain Parquet file. The documents are ordinary row groups, and the full-text and vector indexes are spliced in as byte regions just before the Parquet footer, located by keys in the footer’s metadata. DuckDB or PyArrow or any other Parquet reader can read this file as a normal Parquet file. Because each section’s byte offsets are recorded in the metadata, any section of a superfile can be fetched with a single ranged GET.
The manifest
Each supertable has a manifest, which lists the superfiles that make up the supertable. A write creates new superfiles, writes a new manifest that includes them, and then atomically swaps a small pointer file to the new manifest, so readers always see a consistent set of superfiles.
The byte offsets of the full-text and vector indexes are stored in the Parquet footer, i.e. at the end of the superfile. The full-text index also has a small header that a reader needs before it can look up any term. If a query reads these from every superfile, it would cost an extra GET per superfile before any search work even starts. So, the manifest stores the Parquet footer and index headers of every superfile inline. The manifest is usually cached, and since it already holds the Parquet footer and the index headers, opening a superfile needs no GET at all. The first GET a query makes to a superfile fetches data it actually needs, such as postings of a term. This reduces the cold cost of each superfile from two round trips to one.
The manifest also stores column statistics for every superfile, such min, max, and null count of each column. A query with a filter like created_at > '2026-10-01' can skip a superfile whose max created_at is older than that, without opening it. However, column statistics can’t tell whether a superfile contains the word “refund”, which is what the term index described in the next section is for.
The term index
Without a term index, a full-text query has to ask every superfile whether it contains the query’s terms. That requires reading each superfile’s term dictionary, which means at least one GET per superfile, even for superfiles that turn out not to have the term at all. A supertable can have thousands of superfiles, so this gets expensive quickly.
So, each supertable also has a term index, which lists every term along with the superfiles it appears in. For each term and superfile, it stores (a) the number of documents in that superfile that contain the term, (b) a score bound, i.e. the highest BM25 score the term can give any document in that superfile, and (c) the byte offset of the term’s postings inside the superfile. The term index is split into slices by term range, so a query fetches only the slices that hold its terms, not the whole index.
With this, a query for “refund” first looks up “refund” in the term index, and finds that only sf-03 and sf-06 contain it. It skips every other superfile without opening it. Since the term index also has the byte offset of the postings, the query fetch

hn.title: Show HN: I reverse engineered serum 2 and build an open source alternative
0/1 Knapsack Problem in PyTorch
hn.text:
← main page
pytorch algorithms compilers optimization
Use 20x less peak RAM with dp_knapsack_sliding_hirschberg, a new activation memory budget solver for PyTorch
TL;DR: If you use a default
torch._functorch.config.activation_memory_budget_solver=dp, you can change it to dp_knapsack_sliding_hirschberg
and decrease your peak RAM usage during memory planning by a factor of 20.
What?
When PyTorch builds a computation graph of your ML model, it tries many different things to make it fast and
memory efficient. One technique is to take a joint forward and backward computation graph and choose which
operations should be saved (stored in a memory and reused) and which operations should be recomputed.
Each operation takes some time to run and takes up some memory if stored and we only can use a limited amount
of memory.
0/1 Knapsack problem
Imagine you are a thief and you just broke into a place with many valuable things inside. You have a knapsack
that can carry up to 10 kilograms. You want to maximize the value of things you steal. Ideally, you'd just take
all of them. But if you put more than 10kg to your knaspack, it will break and you will get away with nothing.
Alternatively, you can use some heuristics to pick the items (like take only small items or only green ones),
but then your solution
might not be optimal - you
will steal some
value, but perhaps less than what you could gain in an optimal choice. For your rescue, there come 0/1
knapsack solvers. There are different algorithms that compute optimal items choice within a given capacity (max
weight of things in a knapsack) and given a list of items, where each of items has a value and a cost (weight).
In PyTorch, this is what we actually do, which is: within a RAM budget (knapsack capacity), we choose which
operations (items) should be saved to
the memory to maximize the time savings in runtime (value).
dp_knapsack
Currently, the default implementation of knapsack solver in PyTorch is dp_knapsack, which is a dynamic
programming approach to
solving 0/1 knapsack. The algoritmh is actually simple once you understand it. It helps a lot if you have had a
prior experience with dynamic
programming (I do not). Look at this nice GIF from Wikipedia:
By RDSEED - Own work ,
CC
BY-SA 4.0 , Link
On the left, there is a list of 4 items. i is an index, v is a value and w is a weight. Units irrelevant.
Capacity is 6. That's why on the right side there are 6 columns (each column is a part of total capacity)
and 4 rows (one per item). Ok, actually there are 7 and 5, because of padding with zeros, but that's only
for a computation convenience (every row and column has a parent, index arithmetic gets much easier). You could
actually do it without padding, but I tried and fallbacked to padding anyways, because index arithmetic was a
bit annoying. The table on the
right is called a DP table. It's where the computation happens.
Building a DP table
DP 0/1 Knapsack algorithm goes like this: get an item. In a DP table, go through a corresponding row, column
by
column and compare your item's value to value in current DP table cell (row, column; current column index is
current max weight
(capacity) of your knapsack). If your item's weight is bigger than current column's index, move on to the
next column. If your
item weight is equal to a column index and your item value is higher than current cell, replace the cell
with your item value. If your item weight is smaller than column index and it fits in a spare capacity,
add
it to the cell's value (a free capacity is current capacity minus capacity of picked items). Repeat until you
iterate
through all the items. At this point, you learn what is the maximum value you can get within the weight
budget. If our goal would be to measure a max possible value, then we would stop at this point. Unfortunately,
we
want to know more.
Backtracking
We need to know which items we should take to get this max possible value. So in case of PyTorch, which
operations which we should save to memory and which operations we should recompute. To find out which items
contribute to the max value (in other words, which items were chosen during building DP table), we need to go
backwards through the DP table. We go from the last row and last column upward. We compare a cell with a cell
above (same column, previous row). If they are different, then the current item
contributes to the max value - because each row corresponds to a single item. If they are equal, this
item
will not be stored in a memory and becomes recomputable. Now, we traverse the DP table upward. If the item was
chosen, we move upward by a single row and we
move the position of
the current cell to the left by the
weight of the chosen item. If item wasn't chosen, we move upward by a single row and we start on the
same position as previously. Repeat until we get to the top of the DP table.
Optimization
This solver works correctly. It provides an exact solution and for most of the time you don't need anything
better.
By better I mean 1. faster and 2. less memory hungry. Because look again at the algorithm and the GIF above.
There are
a few issues with it. To get a result, we allocate a full 2D table of shape=(number of items, max_weight), which
is
not great. Horace He (Chillee) who
originally built a great part of (all of?) the memory planning in PyTorch left a note in the DP knapsack solver code:
# TODO(chilli): I think if needed, this memory can be optimized with sliding
# window trick + Hirschberg trick:
# https://codeforces.com/blog/entry/47247?#comment-316200
What he proposes are two optimizations.
Sliding window
Window trick means that instead of building the a DP table, we slide
over a table and use only a previous row and a current row. When moving to the next row, next becomes a new
current and old current becomes a previous row. This improvement alone would be enough, if we wanted to just
compute the max value of items out
of
our list, within a given capacity. But again, we

hn.title: A story of WiFi secrets, UART lockdowns and a damaged flash memory chip
hn.text:
Dear Fell owl ship, just as we announced in our previous post, our beloved God Debugger has seen fit to cast his divine light -laden with opcodes- upon his humble servant, and we have a new homily here in our temple. Please, take a seat and listen to the story of how one of our owls, along with his brother-in-law, moved on to dissect the next component of the Eufy ecosystem: the Eufy HomeBase 2.
Prayers at the foot of the Altar a.k.a. disclaimer
We focused our analysis in Eufy Homebase2 instead of Homebase3 because, as we explained in From your doorbell to your home network it’s the version that I found deployed in my city, and also was the easiest to buy. The firmware version we analyze here is 3.4.2.2h (2026-06-05 18:45:48)
This is the first time I touched something related to “hardware”. I always did vuln hunting on firmwares that I could download from internet, so please forgive the sins I commited
IMPORTANT!!! You must read first the previous article before you continue reading this one.
Table of contents
Just as with the previous article, we will be covering a variety of topics here; consequently, some members of this fellowlship may have no interest in certain sections and might wish to skip straight to whatever appeals to them most. That is why we present this blessed offering: a table of contents.
0x00 Firmware extraction . Description of how the firmware was extracted (and how we damaged part of the flash memory).
0x01 Identifying the Wifi credential generation algorithm . Reverse Engineering the algorithm used to generate the Wifi credential for OCEAN_XXXXXX management wifi.
0x02 Rubber-hose treatment to the UART lockdown . Reflashing a backdoored U-Boot image to get a shell via UART.
0x03 Filesystem gardening for debugging purposes . Recovery image is limited so some filesystem quirks are needed in order to run the main binary.
0x04 Final Words . I share the lack of enthusiasm for writing articles in the age of AI.
0x00 Firmware extraction
In the previous chapter of this saga , I mentioned that we were only able to extract the doorbell’s firmware because the Homebase’s flash memory was soldered directly to the board and did not expose any pins to which we could attach test hooks to dump the firmware. Initially we did not want to desolder it (although in the end we had to as I will explain later) so I had to wait to acquire additional hardware. Craig S. Blackie pointed me to spring clips that would suit the size needed for the Winbond 25Q256JWEQ (WSON8 8.6mm). Once the clip arrived I created the most makeshift setup imaginable, using rubber bands to secure the clip while I proceeded to take readings using the Raspberry Pi’s SPI0 interface, just as we did with the doorbell.
Setup using rubber bands to read the firmware. I performed three reads and the three had different checksums, which usually is a indicator of something being wrong. After inspecting the dumps, I quickly realized they were garbage and completely useless. Unlike with the doorbell, in this case, the power supplied for the read operation also activated other components on the board that interacted with the memory; therefore, to extract the firmware, we had to desolder the chip and read it off-board.
My brother-in-law ( Óscar Lestón ) was the brave soul that desoldered the flash memory (I was too scared to even try it):
Desoldering Although the memory module looked terrible once removed, it was barely damaged…
Extracted flash memory And finally we replicated the same setup using the Raspberry Pi SPI 0 to dump the firmware. This time the three dumps had the same checksum and contained “interesting data”. The only problem was… a block of 64kbs was erased / could not be read, highly probable because we damaged it when extracting the chip.
Using the Raspberry Pi to read the chip off-board Most of the firmware could be extracted using Binwalk.

hn.title: GLP-1 may slow biological aging
hn.text:
June 11, 2026
Susanne Clara Bard , UC San Diego
Semaglutide, a widely used weight loss drug sometimes sold as Ozempic or Wegovy, slowed biological aging across multiple epigenetic clocks in a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trial.
Credit: iStock/Eduardo Monroy Husillos
Beyond the widespread attention GLP-1 drugs are receiving for treating obesity, lowering blood sugar and decreasing the risk of cardiovascular disease, emerging research is investigating their other potential impacts — including their effects on aging.
Now, a new study provides the first randomized, placebo-controlled clinical evidence that semaglutide, a widely used GLP-1 drug, slows down the accumulation of biological aging markers in the DNA of adults with HIV. The study is published in Nature Communications .
Researchers at the University of California, San Diego and several partner institutions analyzed data from a previously published clinical trial of 108 adults with HIV‑associated lipohypertrophy, a condition in which excess fat builds up around the abdomen. About half of the participants received weekly injections of semaglutide, with the rest receiving placebo injections.
The team used a set of biological “epigenetic clocks” to track cellular aging over the 32-week treatment period. These clocks detect DNA methylation, chemical marks on DNA that help regulate how genes are turned on or off without changing the genetic sequence itself. By measuring changes in these marks, the team could assess whether the treatment was associated with a slower or faster biological aging pattern.
People with HIV often experience accelerated aging, even if it is well-controlled with antiretroviral therapy, according to first author Michael Corley, Ph.D., associate professor at UC San Diego School of Medicine and the Stein Institute for Research on Aging . However, the study found compared to the placebo group:
Participants treated with semaglutide exhibited a broad pattern of slower biological aging across epigenetic clocks linked to inflammation and blood, brain, heart, kidney, liver and metabolic health.
The drug slowed the pace of biological aging by 9 %, as measured by the DunedinPACE epigenetic clock.
The drug significantly slowed biological processes associated with the risk of all‑cause mortality and age-related disease, as measured by the PCGrimAge epigenetic clock.
Research suggests there are several mechanisms by which semaglutide may influence biological aging. By reducing inflammation and metabolic stress, GLP-1 drugs decreased chronic immune activation, a primary driver of accelerated aging in people with HIV. They also reduce visceral and ectopic fat that accumulates around the abdomen and organs, which may help curb the inflammatory and metabolic signals that promote aging.
“Emerging data also suggest that GLP-1 drugs may reprogram certain cells in different organs, which could help explain why we see effects across multiple aging clocks,” said Corley.
While the study focused on people with HIV‑associated lipohypertrophy, Corley says it may also offer lessons for the wider population.
“Many of the biological processes we study in HIV are also central to aging in the general population,” he said. “Because these processes can emerge earlier or be more pronounced in people with HIV, this community can help us identify interventions that may improve healthspan more broadly.”
We are not saying that semaglutide reverses aging or makes people younger. What we are seeing is a signal that it may slow some of the biological processes associated with aging.
Michael Corley, Ph.D.
In a related pilot study published in npj Aging last month, Corley and another team of researchers found that taking semaglutide for 24 weeks:
Reduced the rate of biological aging for 42% of participants with HIV and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) — also known as fatty liver disease — as measured by the DunedinPACE epigenetic clock. Those participants also had a greater reduction in liver fat compared with participants whose pace of aging sped up.
Slowed aging associated with the risk of all‑cause mortality in 34% of participants as measured by the PCGrimAge epigenetic clock.
Increased the length of telomeres — repetitive DNA sequences at the ends of chromosomes that protect genetic material — in nearly 49 % of participants as measured by the PCDNAmTL epigenetic clock. Those participants also tended to walk faster after treatment, suggesting better physical function.
Together, these studies add to growing evidence that GLP-1 drugs may influence pathways involved in biological aging.
“We are not saying that semaglutide reverses aging or makes people younger,” said Corley. “What we are seeing is a signal that it may slow some of the biological processes associated with aging. With newer GLP-1–based therapies now emerging, the field has an opportunity to test whether different drugs in this class have distinct effects on aging biology and to identify which patients may benefit most.”
Larger clinical trials are needed to confirm the findings, determine how long treatment effects last, and establish optimal dosing and treatment duration for both people with HIV and the broader population. Future studies will also be needed to test whether the effects of GLP-1 effects on aging biology are enhanced when combined with lifestyle interventions such as diet, exercise and sleep optimization.
The Stein Institute for Research on Aging plans to translate these results into individualized “aging dashboards” to track biological aging with epigenetic clocks, enabling clinicians to design personalized therapies that target the underlying mechanisms of aging and help prevent age‑related diseases.
Additional co-authors on the Nature Communications study include: Alina P. S. Pang at UC San Diego;  Varun Dwaraka and Ryan Smith at TruDiagnostic; Danielle Labbato and Grace A. McComsey at University Hospitals Cleveland Medic

hn.title: OpenAI discloses four more rogue incidents
hn.text:
OpenAI has added four more cases of misbehaving AI agents to a disclosures page it stood up following the Hugging Face hack in July, in an effort to be more transparent.
Recommended Video
The incidents OpenAI disclosed this week all occurred in June, but OpenAI was not aware of three of them until months later in August or September.
Of the 19 total incidents OpenAI details on the disclosure page, most occurred in May or June, but OpenAI did not discover or disclose them until months later. The earliest incident is from January, and the most recent is from Oct. 6.
All of the incidents are examples of what AI researchers call “misalignment,” which is when an AI model fails to follow instructions or takes actions that the person developing the model did not authorize and would not have wanted the model to take. There is no known, silver-bullet solution to preventing this behavior, and it is an active area of research.
Downloading 24 years of unauthorized hospital bed data
Of the four cases OpenAI uploaded this week, it marked two as “critical.” In one of the critical cases , an internal model that was “highly persistent” downloaded 24 years of hospital bed data from an unnamed government website without permission. OpenAI did not immediately respond to Fortune’ s request for comment on which government website it was.
The website initially blocked the agent’s request, but the AI ultimately found a way to bypass the access controls. Multiple times along the way, the agent’s “chain of thought,” in which an agent writes down its reasoning steps, indicated that the model itself was questioning if its actions were “ethical,” but it ultimately proceeded.
On OpenAI’s side, another AI model that acted as an automated grader of the research task the other AI model was trying to fulfill did not consistently flag this behavior as problematic. It “marked some responses incorrect and others correct,” the report said. The way graders assess AI behavior can shape whether it occurs again. In a Sept. 11 essay on misalignment by Turing Award–winner Yoshua Bengio, he said the Hugging Face incident may have occurred because automated graders rewarded cheating and hacking in previous training runs.
“With the OpenAI agents, there is reason to believe successful cheating was actually rewarded: When the scoring program does not see the cheating, it pays out anyway, and such cheats become more likely next time,” Bengio said.
OpenAI says it has since improved its security as well as its alignment grading. “In response to this and to other incidents, we’ve strengthened our security controls, blocked models from accessing the live internet during training or evaluation, improved our alignment grading, and extended our misalignment monitoring to all reinforcement learning and evaluation traffic,” the company noted.
The most recent incident OpenAI has disclosed, which occurred on Oct. 6, involved one of the AI models the company uses as an automated grader. In that case, the grader tried to upload fraudulent reports on what it had found in an evaluation. This is an example of why relying on AI models to grade the training runs of other AI models can be problematic.
Making an unauthorized purchase with someone else’s cryptocurrency
In another disclosed case , a model in the GPT-5.6 Sol family—the predecessor to OpenAI’s current flagship model, GPT-6 Astra—accessed a cryptocurrency wallet the human testers had not provided it, and made an unauthorized payment to complete a task during testing. This occurred on June 26. OpenAI discovered it in September.
“The model questioned whether it had permission” to make the purchase, OpenAI said, again referring to what the model had recorded about its own reasoning in its chain of thought. It then reasoned with itself that since it found the information publicly, it could use it. In the model’s chain-of-thought logs, it figured that since the wallet it found was public, that “funds could be stolen anytime.”
It then concluded, “We can deploy!” It later asked itself again if the act was done “ethically,” and reasoned that the funds were “effectively abandoned.”
Getting internet access, changing live systems
The other incident OpenAI flagged as critical involved a model looking up public data, which theoretically is acceptable, but in the process it accessed the organization’s internal system, made changes to it, and was still able to “retain access … even after reverting the changes,” OpenAI said. It also downloaded 147,451 rows from nonpublic data tables. Perhaps most concerningly, the model did not disclose any of its actions to the evaluators.
In the final case OpenAI disclosed, an AI agent was able to get internet access from a research environment that should have been isolated—potentially similar to what happened during the Hugging Face incident, in which hundreds of AI agents were able to get internet access, although OpenAI did not directly compare these two incidents.
In the newly disclosed case, the agent knew it was not allowed to access the web, so it asked “external services” to perform actions it was blocked from doing. It did this even after it had found another way to answer the question, and also continued to develop its crafty work-around even after completing the task.
Fortune Daily breaks the traditional barrier between audience and newsroom. The show transforms Fortune ’s trusted reporting into actionable, conversational, and entertaining insights for an emerging class of business leaders. Watch here.

hn.title: Amazon uses AI to monitor union risk in UK warehouses
hn.text:
Garfield Hylton has long known that Amazon monitors and logs every minute of his working day. Every product he scans, every second he takes between scans, every time his scanner is briefly inactive – all of it is tracked, recorded, and used to set productivity targets and predictions.
But what 62-year-old Hylton didn’t know is that Amazon seemingly also monitors potential “dissent” in the Coventry warehouse where he works, using AI to surveil posts on social media and the company’s internal staff bulletin board.
Internal documents made public as part of a court battle between Amazon and a Canadian union suggest the tech giant uses Atlas, an in-house AI forecasting tool, to predict how likely its warehouse staff in the US, Canada and the UK are to attempt to form a union, stage a sit-in, or conduct other “disruptive labour events”.
The documents, which appear to be training resources for Amazon managers in Canada, contain an appendix stating Atlas amasses “hundreds of data points” – including posts on Reddit forums and employees’ responses to internal feedback surveys, as well as wider information on the workplace and any previous industrial action – to award warehouses a risk score of between 100 and 900 for union activity.
The lower the score, the more likely Atlas believes workers – whom Amazon calls ‘associates’ – in that warehouse are to unionise or take other actions that could impact Amazon’s productivity or profitability. The document states that for the company’s leadership, higher scores are “better”.
This “makes it clear that they think the union is bad”, Michael Newman, a partner at London-based law firm Leigh Day, told openDemocracy. Newman said it tells “a very different story” from Amazon’s previous assertions that it does not seek to prevent workers from joining a union.
Warehouses appear to be categorised into five tiers based on their Atlas score, where Tier 5 is “no immediate perceived risk” and Tier 1 is “future activity is imminent”. The document suggests this scale can be used to “inform staffing decisions, resource planning, standard actions, and ownership to mitigate risks to Amazon labour structure”.
An Amazon spokesperson refuted the characterisation of Atlas as “individual employee monitoring or surveillance”, stating: “This is site/building level activity only.”
They added that the company does “not track individual employees’ opinions, affiliations or union membership”, or any “personal data”, and said Atlas is not used to monitor dissent, but to “help us understand where associates need more support and to ensure we’re addressing issues that they raise”.
In total, 16 Amazon warehouses across the US, Canada and the UK are “Tier 1”, according to the document. Two are in the UK: a £500m robotic-fulfilment centre in Sutton Coldfield, north-east Birmingham (referred to by Amazon as EMA4), and the warehouse where Hylton works near Coventry (BHX4).
An Amazon US employee is surveyed on their feelings "about the future of AI at Amazon". Source: Facebook Hylton, whose role involves receiving goods into the warehouse and dispatching them on to other warehouses, is a member of the GMB union. He believes the extent of the data Amazon has collected on his colleagues creates a huge power imbalance, with workers having only their own experiences to defend themselves.
“It’s not right in a democracy… the employer should not be interfering,” he said, speaking to openDemocracy soon after learning about the Atlas tool from GMB. “Workers should be allowed to decide if they wish to choose to unionise,” he continued, adding: “If you're then monitoring, you're undermining a process deliberately and willfully.”
Rachel Fagan, an organiser for GMB, told openDemocracy: “It’s quite clear from these documents that these sites are being monitored for union activity. Everyone knows that Amazon is heavy on surveillance, but this becomes more personal.
“Amazon is using this technology to essentially outwit or manoeuvre workers that want to organise [a union]. Nothing in this fight against Amazon is an even playing field; they have all the wealth, all the technology, everything to their disposal and they use it,” she added.
GMB has long tried to unionise Amazon workers in the UK, coming closest to winning formal recognition in Coventry in July 2024. Employees at the warehouse became the first in the country to take strike action against Amazon in January 2023, and around 2,600 took part in an official ballot for union recognition at the site six months later, which GMB lost by just 28 votes .
The union and Foxglove, a tech justice non-profit, have accused Amazon of using “dirty tricks” to swing the vote in its favour. These include the mass hiring of non-unionised workers and allegedly plastering QR codes that employees could scan to cancel their GMB membership over screens, cafeteria tables, and toilet doors in the warehouse in the run-up to the vote.
Foxglove and Leigh Day are representing two workers in a legal challenge against Amazon’s use of ‘click-to-quit’ QR codes. They argue that the tool was an attempt to “bully” workers into ending their union membership.
The documents revealing Amazon’s Atlas AI tool were disclosed as part of a legal challenge by Canadian union Unifor and shared with US non-profit publication Truthout . The British Columbia Labour Board ultimately ruled that Amazon had violated multiple local labour laws , following an earlier ruling that found the company had unlawfully imposed a wage freeze on unionised workers at a warehouse outside Vancouver.
Rosa Curling, co-executive director of Foxglove, described the level of surveillance detailed in the document as “highly intrusive”, showing that Amazon has a “very intentional policy to try and bust organising, bust unionising efforts, and they are using all sorts of tools to do that”.
Curling continued: “We are actively reviewing these documents to see what additional arguments, if any, we should be adding to our existing

hn.title: Intuitive concurrent programming in any language
hn.text:
Build predictable , concurrent , time-sensitive , and distributed systems.
Lingua Franca is a coordination language for efficient, deterministic, multi-threaded, time-sensitive, embedded, and distributed programs. The result of decades of research, it offers more repeatable behavior than other concurrent programming frameworks, including threads, pub-sub, actors, and service-oriented architectures.
Get Started Read the Docs
Deterministic Concurrency
Lingua Franca offers a straightforward way to write deterministic multi-threaded and distributed applications, eliminating concerns about thread management, synchronization, and race conditions.
Built-in Timing Semantics
Timing is embedded within Lingua Franca's core, empowering developers to handle time-sensitive tasks with precision and without the complex timing logic typically required in concurrent programming.
Simplified Distribution
Lingua Franca enables seamless transition from single to distributed system architectures with minimal modifications, abstracting away the complexities of distributed systems programming.
Architect your application in LF
import Player from "../Player.lf"
main reactor RockPaperScissors {
// Instantiate two Player reactors here
player1 = new Player (id = 1 )
player2 = new Player (id = 2 )
// Make connections between them
player2 . reveal -> player1 . observe
player1 . reveal -> player2 . observe
}
A New Programming Paradigm
Lingua Franca is the first reactor-oriented coordination language. It allows you to specify reactive components and compose them. Lingua Franca eliminates race conditions by construction, makes it easy to specify timed behavior, and removes the need to perform manual synchronization.
Consider a game of "rock paper scissors" where two players need to reveal their choice simultaneously. In Lingua Franca, "at the same time" has a clear and precise meaning. This makes the implementation simple and intuitive, and guarantees it to be fair. If the Player class were to observe the other's choice before revealing its own, Lingua Franca's causality analysis would find a causality loop and tell you that the program is invalid.
Not a New Programming Language
With Lingua Franca, you forget about thread libraries or message passing middlewares, but you continue using the languages you like. The bodies of reactive code that make up the functionality of reactors are written in the programming language of your choice. We currently support C, C++, Python, TypeScript, and Rust.
Open-source and Supported by Research
Lingua Franca was first developed at UC Berkeley where it was influenced by decades worth of research in models of computation.
Shortly after its inception, researchers from Kiel University and TU Dresden joined the team, contributing diagram synthesis and layout technology, highly-efficient runtime implementations, and various compiler improvements. Since then, we have worked with real-time systems experts from UT Dallas, embedded systems specialists from NTNU, and networking and security researchers from Hanyang University and ASU.

hn.title: FLUX 3 Image Klein
hn.text:
Back to blog Models
News
Research
FLUX 3 Image Klein
Today we are releasing FLUX 3 Image Klein, a 5.6B parameter open weights model for text-to-image generation, image editing and multi-reference generation with up to 10 reference images. It shares core capabilities with the full FLUX 3 Image model: native 4K generation, pixel-perfect editing, and bounding boxes that control where elements are placed or confine edits to a defined area.
FLUX 3 Image Klein builds on FLUX 3's shared learnings across images, video and audio. Images contribute spatial detail, video adds motion and physical dynamics, and audio provides information about events and interactions. Together, these signals help the model generate images that feel grounded in the real world.
The release includes a base model for fine-tuning and a step distilled model for low-latency generation, along with FP8, INT8 and NVFP4 builds developed with NVIDIA support, under the FLUX Kommunity License.
Try it in the BFL API · Download the weights
Leading open weights quality with fewer parameters
In internal evaluations, FLUX 3 Image Klein ranks first in text-to-image, multi-reference generation and image editing, ahead of larger open weights models. It also rates above the closed models in the comparison, Ideogram V4.5 and FLUX.2 [pro]. At 5.6B parameters, it is the smallest open model in the comparison, against 7B for Qwen-Image 2.1 and 12.9B for Krea 2. Compared with FLUX.2 [klein] 9B, it gains 91 Elo in text-to-image and 70 in image editing, with 38% fewer parameters.
FLUX 3 Image Klein was also optimized for consumer GPUs. Fewer parameters make it practical to run locally and cheaper to adapt, and teams with data sovereignty or local deployment requirements can evaluate and adapt the model on their own infrastructure. This is also key for on-device image editing, allowing consumers to edit images directly on their favorite laptops. The generator weights require 11.2 GB in BF16 and 5.6 GB in FP8. With the INT8 build, FLUX 3 Image Klein runs on NVIDIA GeForce RTX GPUs with as little as 8GB of VRAM, through ComfyUI or Diffusers, extending what FLUX.2 [klein] started to even smaller hardware. With the distilled model and the INT8 build, it generates a 1MP image in about 4 seconds on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090 and under 9 seconds on an RTX 4070 through ComfyUI.
Generation time by GPU: Step-distilled model, 16 steps. Seconds per image, one image per run. Lower is better. Measured by NVIDIA; RTX results in ComfyUI; data results are the best-performing framework for each configuration. Each GPU shows its quickest build. Generation time on the GPU itself; API latency in Section 02 also includes queueing, network and prompt upsampling. Generation time by GPU: Base model, 50 steps. Seconds per image, one image per run. Lower is better. Measured by NVIDIA; RTX results in ComfyUI. Each GPU shows its quickest build. The base checkpoint is built for fine-tuning: Diffusers and Ostris's AI Toolkit support LoRA training from day one, and NVIDIA's NeMo AutoModel ships recipes that work directly from the released checkpoints.
For even faster production workloads that need lower latency, we also work with teams on specific customizations that get you there. Get in touch .
On the speed–quality frontier
FLUX 3 Image Klein also extends the speed–quality Pareto frontier. Through the BFL API, it delivers lower latency than Qwen-Image 2.1, FLUX.2 [pro], Ideogram V4.5 and Krea 2, and the highest rating at its latency and above. In the charts below, the violet line traces the highest rating available at each latency and the gray line shows the previous frontier.
Latency is measured end to end, from request submission to the finished 1 MP image, including queueing. FLUX 3 Image Klein was timed on our servers. Other models were timed from the client, which includes polling and network time. Krea 2 was timed on its Medium tier; its Large tier took 31.1 seconds for text-to-image.
Get started
FLUX 3 Image Klein is available today as open weights and through the BFL API .
Try it
BFL API: the distilled model is available as flux-3-image-klein, with prompt upsampling and pixel restoration, which preserves unedited regions of an image exactly. Pricing starts at $0.009 per 1K image.
Playground or Hugging Face .
Build with it
Weights on Hugging Face: base and distilled .
Reference inference code , including a Gradio demo for bounding-box control.
Try it out on Hugging Face Spaces .
Day-one support in ComfyUI , Hugging Face Diffusers , TensorRT-LLM , SGLang Diffusion and vLLM-Omni .
LoRA training with Ostris's AI Toolkit and recipes in NVIDIA NeMo AutoModel .
Trained on NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 and optimized for NVIDIA's accelerated computing platform, serving through NVIDIA TensorRT LLM, vLLM-Omni and SGLang Diffusion .
On NVIDIA GB300, the distilled model generates a 1MP image in under 0.6 seconds in NVFP4. Serving a LoRA adds around 5% to generation time.
License
The weights are available under the FLUX Kommunity License, which allows free commercial use for individuals and companies with annual revenue under $5M, alongside research and non-commercial use. Larger organizations can deploy commercially through our self-hosted licensing options or API.
Safety
In an effort to make AI technology both open and safe, we implement multiple safeguards throughout the model development lifecycle to combat misuse. These include dataset filters during pre-training to limit exposure to harmful content, and targeted fine-tuning during post-training to suppress harmful behaviors, making it progressively harder to elicit harmful content. Ahead of the release, the FLUX 3 Image Klein checkpoints were rigorously red teamed internally and evaluated by our external safety partner Cinder, demonstrating substantially fewer vulnerabilities than other popular open weights models. More on our safety methodology is available here .

Florida Hams Provide Communications Support During Hurricane Isaias
Amateur radio operators from Florida’s Santa Rosa, Nassau, Lake, Pinellas, and Leon Counties played an important role in supporting emergency communications efforts during and following Hurricane Isaias, helping ensure that critical communication capabilities remained available throughout the storm.
In Santa Rosa County, volunteer amateur radio operators staffed the Emergency Operations Center (EOC) and the evacuation shelter at the Milton Community Center. These volunteers provided a communications link between the shelter and the EOC, relaying situational updates and maintaining readiness to support emergency communications should traditional systems become unavailable.
Amateur radio operators across the state also supported auxiliary communications efforts, providing additional capabilities to maintain contact with the State Emergency Operations Center in Tallahassee if conventional communication networks experienced disruptions.
"While traditional communications systems have become significantly more reliable over the years, amateur radio continues to serve as a dependable auxiliary communications resource," said Arc Thames, W4CPD, Santa Rosa County Community Emergency Response Team (CERT) and Amateur Radio Emergency Service (ARES) Program Manager. "When disaster strikes, our volunteers are trained, prepared, and ready to step in wherever we're needed. It's another layer of resiliency that helps protect our communities."
Thames also serves as the ARRL Northern Florida Section Emergency Coordinator and the Amateur Radio Liaison to the Florida Division of Emergency Management, supporting the coordination of amateur radio and auxiliary communications resources statewide.
"During tropical weather events impacting Florida, our Auxiliary Communications team provides volunteer operators to monitor amateur radio communications at the State Emergency Operations Center in Tallahassee," Thames explained. "This ensures that if someone is unable to reach emergency officials through traditional means, we have another way to receive and relay critical information. We always hope we're not needed, but we're glad to be there just in case when all else fails." — Thanks to ARRL Northern Florida SEC Arc Thames, W4CPD, for the above

hn.title: We still use paper
hn.text:
Thousands of years and several technological revolutions later, we still use paper to think and write. In this age of AI, we still use paper, we still use keyboards which evolved from typewriters, and we still use word processors on our computers with them.
This is not a Luddite take. I think AI is here to stay. To reject AI for the wrong uses, or to prefer old technologies for the right uses, is not being a luddite.
To what degree will AI replace existing tools and technologies?
Paper was replaced by successive technologies for many uses, but not all of them. Each technology has inherent qualities. The tools we use in our work influence the output we create. We need to know what is it we want to make, then select the right tool for the job.
AI is a revolutionary technology, but its simplest tool form—chat—isn’t going to be the best interface for most tasks. This is why throwing a bunch of compute at problems, especially domain-specific problems, can feel so inefficient and frustrating. It’s why arming AI with tool calls and harnesses have been so good for achieving useful results. From the opposite end, existing software can be built upon to incorporate AI for better results too.
When the computing revolution first rolled around, some people perhaps tried to use MS-DOS as a writing tool (I’m guessing, I was five). We then built upon that to create the word processor. Likewise for AI revolution, we have to build more sophisticated, considered products and services that best leverage it, and design ways to corral and encourage productive and useful results.
We should use new tools and technology to do things that weren't possible before. We can be curious but not confined to using new technology to do things. We can mold and refine technology so that it suits our usage. We have agency in all of these choices.
Each prior technology has its own use and place.
AI will enable and replace many things, but it’ll never replace paper.
I write about doing my life's work and living up to my potential as a solopreneur: subscribe to THPC on Substack . This article was written with WriteMapper , a mind-mapping desktop app for thinking and writing, available on macOS and Windows.

When No ID Means No Internet
hn.text:
Español
This post was co-authored by Sheila B. Lalwani , a doctorate student and recent COMPASS Fellow hosted by EFF.
Age verification proposals are often presented as a simple tradeoff: sacrifice a little privacy to better safeguard children online. But that framing overlooks a more fundamental question. What happens to people who cannot verify their age at all? This is particularly a problem when users are required to prove their age with identity documents.
Age-related restrictions are developing quickly around the world. While they differ radically across jurisdictions, in the past year, we’ve witnessed a sharp uptick toward mandatory age assurance for social media access but also for other high-risk digital services.
For example:
In late 2025, Australia became the first country to implement a minimum age requirement for prohibiting children under age 16 from creating or holding social media accounts.
India passed the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act that includes mandatory verifiable parental consent and has undertaken ongoing discussions for social media restriction.
The United Kingdom passed the Online Safety Act requiring age verification across a swath of services hosting content considered harmful to users under 18. More than half the states across the U.S. have enacted age verification laws .
An EU Commission ’s expert report recommends a ban on social media access for users under 13. It also recommends mandatory age verification for platforms to ensure that users are ‘age appropriate.’
The Access Problem
Age verification laws that are predicated on the necessity of users possessing a current passport, driver’s license, credit card, or similar documents proving their identity exclude critical sections of populations. And this problem is global in nature: Millions of people lack government-issued identification or encounter regular challenges to obtaining or updating it.
Roughly 15 million adult U.S. citizens lack a driver’s license, and a further 2.6 million lack any government photo ID ; leaving large groups blocked from online content or services. The UK has a similar predicament: proof-of-age checks are often reliant on passports, driver’s licenses, or other recognized alternatives, which can pose unique challenges to people without these documents.
Much of the advocacy around age verification discusses the privacy harms of age verification. Yet these measures also threaten something more fundamental: equal access to information and the ability to exercise the right to freedom of expression.
Unfortunately, age verification systems foster unequal access to information and provide an asymmetric solution to find essential information, build community, and weigh in on public discourse. As governments and companies increasingly require users to prove their age before accessing online services, these individuals risk being excluded from large parts of the internet altogether.
Effects on Global Majority Countries
Age verification laws reshape who can speak, who can access information, and who gets excluded from the digital public sphere. In other words, age verification is not a neutral safety measure: it presents a structural barrier to disproportionately exclude certain groups—particularly those in the global majority—and alters the architecture of global online expression. Some of these groups are already marginalized offline, and age verification extends that exclusion into digital spaces.
For instance, 850 million people globally do not have ID . Most of these individuals exist in primarily low and middle income countries in Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia. The World Bank points out that many are members of marginalized groups and more than half of those lacking access to identity documentation also have children whose births have not been registered. Women are particularly vulnerable and are 8% less likely than men to have an ID. Other vulnerable groups, such as adults in low income countries, are less likely to have an ID when they fall below 25 years, as are those with a primary school education or less or those in rural areas.
A policy paper from EDRi points out that age verification laws provide quick tech solutions but overlook longstanding structural challenges and undermine the universality of the internet. The analysis finds that age verification laws have serious human rights implications and ironically harm the very individuals they deem to protect. Moreover, these laws depend on the collection of harmful mass data that human rights organizations, including EFF, is fighting against —and has for decades .
For example:
In Morocco , a push to restrict children’s access would ban under-13s from creating accounts on gaming platforms. This could potentially create challenges for those with IDs that have incomplete information concerning the year of birth. In addition, this push would also impact those who attempt to leave Morocco.
In Egypt , the lack of ID cards has created challenges for minority groups such as the Baha’i.
Stateless individuals would also struggle under age verification laws. The Rohingya , the world’s largest population of stateless people , often lack IDs .
Kuwait’s Bidoon population also lacks proper identification materials. According to Amnesty International , this leads many to rely on standard civil identity cards, which can be restrictive.
Nigeria launched a national program to provide ID cards to its population in 2007. Since then, 64.4 million have registered, but that represents just over 30% of the national population.
The Kafala system, a practice in several countries across the Middle East , also introduces challenges for age verification laws. Under this legal framework, migrant workers’ legal residency and employment status are bound to a specific employer. This potentially leaves stateless persons or migrant workers vulnerable to forced labor and restricted movements.

hn.title: JPEG XL vs. AVIF for web use-cases
hn.text:
JPEG XL vs AVIF for web use-cases
Posted 15 October 2026 JPEG XL has now landed in all major browsers, so I figured I'd take a closer look at what it's good/bad at compared to other formats.
Conclusions
I'll go into full detail, with examples and benchmarks, but for those of you who don't have the time, here are the headlines:
For lossy photos on the web, AVIF almost always produces smaller files than JPEG XL. At default effort settings, the best JPEG XL version is typically 15–25% larger than the equivalent AVIF. At maximum effort settings, the gap narrows a little, to typically 6–20%. There are outliers, where JPEG XL is close to, or even beats AVIF, so if you want the absolute best result for a particular image, it's worth trying both. See the F1 image for a typical example, and the weasel for an outlier.
The JPEG XL encoder matters a lot. jixel , a newer JPEG XL encoder, usually produces smaller files than libjxl , except when the image has detailed transparency. The people image is one example.
For screenshots and illustrations, AVIF is much better than JPEG XL. The equivalent JPEG XL is 30–90% larger at default effort settings, and 20–70% larger at maximum effort settings. Lossy AVIF handles these well - you don't need to use lossless formats unless you really need bit-exact results. See the screenshot and illustration examples.
For images with transparency, AVIF is much better than JPEG XL. The libjxl version is 31–44% larger at default effort settings, and 61–70% larger at maximum effort settings. jixel always encodes transparency losslessly, which makes its files 2–3x the size of AVIF's. See the data .
AVIF is generally faster to encode, and uses less memory, when you factor in file size. jixel is faster than AVIF and uses less memory, but its files are typically significantly larger, so AVIF is better on balance. See the F1 image for one example.
AVIF is faster to decode. JPEG XL typically takes 2–3x as long to decode at medium quality, but the gap narrows at very high qualities, where Chrome can sometimes decode JPEG XL faster. The people image is one example.
Higher effort settings are worth it for AVIF and jixel, but not libjxl. libjxl's higher efforts are much slower, use a lot more memory, and barely improve the result. Sometimes they produce larger files than the default effort. The screenshot is an example of this.
AVIF's 4:2:0 mode (half colour resolution) shouldn't be your default. It rarely reduces file size, and it makes higher qualities harder to reach. Although, it is quicker to encode and decode. Stick with 4:4:4 if you don't have time to check both. The F1 image is one example, and the screenshot is an exception.
Quality settings are reliable for all the encoders. With a single quality setting, the resulting quality varies a bit between images, but all the encoders vary in the same direction, and in ways that seem reasonable. See the data .
Progressive JPEG XL is basically free at high effort. jixel recently added support for early progressive previews, and at its slowest setting they cost little or nothing, but at its default setting the files are 12% bigger. Firefox and Chrome support progressive JPEG XL. Safari still renders the final image, but doesn't show progressive previews. However, is this type of progressive rendering a good user experience? See the examples and data .
AVIF supports progressive rendering! It's Chrome-only for now, but it's in progress for Firefox. It's more complex than progressive JPEG XL, but it gives you more control over what the preview looks like, the files are usually smaller, and they're much faster to decode. See for yourself .
For HDR, JPEG XL lacks gain maps, which is a significant limitation compared to AVIF. The JPEG XL format supports gain maps, but they aren't supported by browser decoders, and the encoding story is messy/experimental. When comparing non-gain mapped HDR content, the two quality metrics I used disagree a lot, but they agree that JPEG XL produces smaller files compared to AVIF. See the examples .
JPEG XL can make existing JPEGs 9–20% smaller, without further loss. It's also as fast or faster to decode, except for small images. See the data .
For lossless, JPEG XL is the clear winner. Lossless WebP is 9–17% larger for photos, and lossless AVIF is 30–120% larger. But lossless images are almost never what you want on the web. If you do use them on the web (like I do on this page), watch out for jixel's higher efforts - it often produces files that are too slow to decode. See the data .
Animated image formats continue to be a dumb idea. Please don't use them. Learn more , if you must.
For web use-cases, I'd currently default to AVIF 4:4:4, with the highest effort level I can be bothered with. If I felt AVIF was producing an unusually large file, I'd take a look at JPEG XL via jixel, and see if it did better.
Both AVIF and JPEG XL (via jixel) have seen massive improvements recently, so it's possible that this recommendation could change in future. There's been a lot of misinformation around this stuff, and your AI will happily deliver that misinformation to you. Instead, test things with your own images.
AVIF folks suggest that JPEG XL is technically limited compared to AVIF. That might be true, but in this article I'm focusing on results with today's implementations.
Methodology
I 'created' a benchmarking script , that encodes images using various codecs at various settings, and records various details.
I'm using the latest released versions of the image codecs, which at time of writing is:
avifenc 1.4.2
libjxl 0.12.0 (using its cjxl encoder)
jixel 0.4.2 (git f487299 ), a second JPEG XL encoder
cwebp 1.6.0 (lossless WebP is used later in the article)
I chose a selection of images, and encoded most of them to a width of 1598 pixels - which is 2x the maximum width images appear on this blog. This means they look sharp on high density displays , which most users have. As a result, if you're viewing this on a smal

hn.title: The Altair 8800 Reborn
hn.text:
The Altair-Duino 8800
I was a child of 9 years old when the Altair 8800 was announced on the pages of Popular Electronics magazine in January of 1975. It captured my imagination - and I knew that someday I would build and own my own computer. I never did get an Altair 8800 - the computer revolution was started and it moved FAST . The heyday of the Altair lasted only a short while. The first computer I built was 6 years later when I built the Sinclair ZX81 kit.
Well imagine my surprise 42 years later when David Hansel of Brookline, MA published his Ardunio-based Altair 8800 emulator project on hackster.io ! I knew this was my chance to finally build an Altair 8800! Sure, there are other Altair 8800 clones out there, but all seemed out of reach for a simple working-man hobbyist. There was Mike Douglas's excellent altairclone.com which is a dead-ringer look-alike for the Altair 8800, also Mike's 8800c which is an Altair with S100 bus built from new components, then there's the very ambitious altairkit.com in which Grant Stockly painstakingly recreated every board and component of an original Altair.
Once I saw David's code and design, I knew I could improve on it and make an affordable, easy-to-build kit. My first "beta-testers" were my 12 and 14 year old sons. Yes, you can still follow David's original plan if you wish. If you want a ready-to-go kit, look no further.
This is a cycle-accurate recreation of the original Altair 8800. What does that mean? It means the Intel 8080 CPU is emulated, as is some of the basic I/O (disk drives, serial ports, etc.) but everything else is REAL Altair machine code and CP/M that was created more than 40 years ago.
Recommended skills: Through-hole soldering and basic electronics familiarity. Estimated build time: 4-6 hours, depending on experience. Required tools: Soldering iron, solder, small side-cutters, Phillips screwdriver, and a computer with a USB terminal program (PuTTY, Tera Term, CoolTerm, Serial2, etc.). Not required but strongly recommended: 7mm hex driver, 8mm hex driver. Original Altair 8800
Dimensions: 17" x 7" x 18"
Weight: depends on cards loaded, but generally around 65 lbs.
RAM: 64KB maximum
Altair-Duino (Pro version)
Dimensions: 17" x 7" x 18"
Weight: 9 lbs without expansion cards.
RAM: 512KB (64KB maximum for Altair emulation, the rest used as storage for Altair programs and utilities.)
What is the Difference Between Pro and Experimenter?
The Altair-Duino Pro is my kit that is housed in Mike Douglas's Altair Clone case. It faithfully emulates both the look and the operation of the original Altair. While it looks great, it does take up a lot of room (and can be quite expensive to ship internationally).
Another option is the shelf-friendly (and budget-friendly) Altair-Duino Experimenter . It has the same functionality of the Pro, but in a more easily displayable form factor that is 15" x 6" x 2.5".
I also have to say "thank you" to Oscar Vermeulen of Obsolescence Guaranteed for his recreation of the PDP-8 , which got me on this quest to recreate historic computers.
Buy The Kit!
The Kit
This is a kit you can probably put together in a Saturday afternoon. Here's what's included:
PC Board
You'll receive a professionally made printed circuit board with all components, ready for you to assemble.
Arduino Due
Arduino's first ARM development board, based on a powerful 32bit CortexM3 ARM microcontroller.
Fully Loaded
Because of the capacity of the Due, it comes pre-loaded with useful and entertaining Altair software.
Take it Further
The source code for the Altair simulator is published under GPLv3, meaning you can experiment and modify the code.
What if I can't get the kit working?
Don't worry, thousands of people have built this kit with no problems at all. We have an active online forum if you have any questions, and I'll personally guarantee you end up with a working kit. If you have problems, you can pay two-way shipping and I'll diagnose and repair the kit for you.
Would you rather build an Altair that is closer to the original, with a real 8080 processor and a functional S100 bus? Good news, the Altair 8800c designed by Mike Douglas is just what you're looking for. You'll need to start with the Altair Reproduction Case then head over to Mike's site for info to source the rest of the parts.

nvidia.title: Be There for the Beginning: Celebrate the Launch of NVIDIA RTX Spark
nvidia.summary: A new beginning for Windows PCs starts tomorrow with the launch of NVIDIA RTX Spark — one PC built for creators, gamers and AI agents. All are invited to celebrate with NVIDIA and partners at launch events around the world. Share Your Spark Every PC has a story. What was your first Windows PC, and […]
nvidia.text:
A new beginning for Windows PCs starts tomorrow with the launch of NVIDIA RTX Spark — one PC built for creators, gamers and AI agents. All are invited to celebrate with NVIDIA and partners at launch events around the world.
Share Your Spark
Every PC has a story. What was your first Windows PC, and what did it spark a love for? Join the celebration online by sharing responses with #ShareYourSpark for a chance to win an ASUS ProArt P14 RTX Spark laptop signed by NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang. See the campaign and official rules .
See What Reviewers Are Saying
From local AI workflows to creative apps and gaming, see what reviewers are saying about RTX Spark — then experience it at a launch celebration.
“The fact that NVIDIA, Microsoft and their partners have delivered such a capable, compatible and polished platform even in its first at-bat should put the rest of the PC industry on notice.” — Tom’s Hardware
“I tested NVIDIA’s RTX Spark for gaming and local AI – the performance absolutely stunned me.” — TrustedReviews , UK
“I’m very happy to report that performance is actually looking really good when it comes to AI, gaming and creative workflows.” — Microcenter
“[RTX Spark] is a different species of computer that has arrived early. It is a statement of intent from NVIDIA about where computing is going — trading raw benchmarking crowns for the ability to carry a self-rewriting, fully autonomous, CUDA-accelerated digital brain in your backpack.” — Tom’s Guide
“One of the most impressive parts of the launch is how many apps NVIDIA has worked with to ensure optimisation with the Spark technology.” — Creative Bloq
Independent testing from Artificial Analysis offers an early look at the powerful local AI performance RTX Spark brings to a laptop.
Join the Launch Celebrations
On Friday, Oct. 16, get hands on with RTX Spark at launch events around the world. Explore demos for creating, developing and gaming, connect with fellow enthusiasts and discover what local AI can do.
Times below are local. Follow each event’s entry instructions. Space is limited.
San Francisco — Best Buy, 1717 Harrison Street, 10 a.m.-12 p.m . Try hands-on demos, meet iJustine and hear fireside conversations with local tech founders. Free, first-come, first-served entry; no ticket required. Event details .
Berlin — Xperion at Saturn, Alexanderplatz 3, 7-10:30 p.m . Explore hands-on demos and stage programming with creators and developers. Registration required. RSVP .
Taipei — Muse Garden, No. 88 Yanchang Road . Join an evening of demos, music and AI community discussions, with shopping and networking continuing until 10:15 p.m. Registration required .
Beijing — JD MALL Beijing Shuangjing Store, No. 31 Guangqu Road . Check in begins at 7 p.m. Launch celebration starts at 8 p.m., followed by hands-on demos. Event concludes at 9:30 p.m. Register through WeChat.
Istanbul — Vatan Bilgisayar Topkapı, Mevlana Caddesi No. 138 . Explore hands-on demos and local creator programming. Walk-in entry; no advance registration required.
Seoul — COEX East Lobby, 513 Yeongdong-daero . Hands-on demos begin at 7 p.m., with gaming and AI creator programming from 8 p.m. Event concludes at 9:30 p.m. No advance registration required.
